I have put a card on every table at these events for nine years, and people always ask me why. So here is the honest answer. A table with no card on it talks about the sessions for about four minutes, and then everybody looks at their phone. That is not a failure of the guests. It is a failure of the question, because there is no question, so the only available subject is the thing everybody just sat through. The card has to ask something impossible. That is the rule I have arrived at. A realistic question gets a realistic answer, and nobody remembers a realistic answer. Nobody at that table has a year off. Nobody is moving to another city on Monday. So they cannot look it up and they cannot check it, and they have to invent, and inventing is the only moment in the evening when people say something that is actually true about themselves. One more thing, and this is the part I enjoy. About half the room says travelling. Travelling is the safe answer. The interesting person at your table is almost always the one who says something else.

There is a small and rather elegant study on how you ask somebody what they think. Two groups, same job offer, same details, same salary. The first group was asked directly whether they would take it. The second group was asked something slightly different: what would you tell a friend to do, if a friend were offered this. Same information, one word of distance. The answers were not slightly different. They were a different kind of answer. The second group talked for longer. They named more disadvantages, and they named them earlier. And when the researchers came back a month later, the second group had changed their minds far less often than the first. The explanation the authors offer is not complicated, and I think it is right. When you ask somebody directly, they have to defend a position in front of you, and defending starts before thinking finishes. A hypothetical costs nothing to admit. Nobody is committed to anything, so they stop protecting a decision they have not taken yet, and simply describe what they actually think.
